lead: Morphing turns one shape or image into another: the outline of a face becomes another face, a letter A becomes a B, a car becomes a tiger. Two things happen together — the geometry moves and the colours cross over. A warp alone gives B's outline painted in A's colours. A fade alone gives A's outline with B's colour. Only both, driven by the same time value, read as one object changing into another. Film titles, advertisements, face-ageing apps and 3D character faces all use it. Some syllabi call it image metamorphosis or shape blending.
prereq: You need: digital images and pixels (Unit 1), linear interpolation as used for in-betweens in 5.2, Bezier curves for morphing outlines (Unit 3), and 2D transformations (Unit 2).

blocks.text: Every morph runs two jobs at once. The geometric job changes the shape of A into the shape of B. The colour job changes A's colours into B's colours.
One number t drives both. t = 0 is the source, t = 1 is the target, and frames at t = 0.1, 0.2, … fill the gap.

The geometric job needs correspondence: a rule saying which part of A is which part of B. You place control points on the source — eye corners, the tip of the nose, the corners of a letter — and mark the matching points on the target. Or you lay a mesh of small triangles over the source and drag its nodes to the matching places on the target. The computer cannot guess that your ear should become the target's ear and not its chin; a person, or a face detector, supplies the pairs.
After that it is arithmetic. Each control point travels a straight line.

blocks.where: P_A is the point's position on the source, P_B its matched position on the target, t the time fraction from 0 to 1, and P(t) the intermediate position. This is the interpolation that fills in-betweens between keyframes (see 5.2), applied to one point instead of a whole drawing.

sections.h3: Moving the pixels: forward and inverse warping

blocks.text: Moving the control points does not move the pixels between them. Two ways to move those.

Forward warping. Visit each source pixel, compute where it lands at time t, write its colour there. When control points move apart, neighbouring source pixels land far from each other and leave unpainted holes. When points crowd together, several source pixels land on one output pixel and all but one are lost.

Inverse warping. Start from the output. For each output pixel, find the source position it came from, read the colour there, write it. The source-to-target map is inverted once, then every output pixel gets exactly one value, so there are no holes. The source position rarely falls on a whole pixel, so the colour is sampled from the nearest four pixels: nearest neighbour for speed, bilinear interpolation (a weighted average) for a smoother frame.

With a mesh, each triangle is warped by its own affine map — the map carrying its three source corners to their three interpolated positions (see Unit 2, 2D transformations). Affine maps keep straight lines straight, so the triangle stays a triangle and the mesh simply deforms. The warped pair is not blended yet; it is handed to the dissolve.

sections.h3: Cross-dissolve, and one t for both jobs

blocks.text: The cross-dissolve is a weighted average of the two warped images, pixel by pixel.

blocks.where: C_A is the colour of the warped source at that pixel, C_B the colour of the warped target at the same pixel, and t the same fraction used by the warp. Red, green and blue are blended separately.

blocks.text: The weights (1 − t) and t always add to 1, so a flat region keeps its brightness as it crosses over; it dims or brightens only if the sum is broken. Both jobs must use the same t. If the warp uses t = 0.3 while the dissolve uses 0.6, outline and shading drift apart — the silhouette sits in one place and its colour in another, and the eye catches it at once.

In 3D the same formula runs on vertices: V(t) = (1 − t)·V_A + t·V_B, where V_A and V_B are matched vertices. Vertex morphing needs identical topology — the same number of vertices with the same faces in the same order — because vertex 47 of A must move to vertex 47 of B. Normals and texture coordinates are interpolated by the same rule, and the interpolated normal is scaled back to unit length before it is used for lighting, so shading follows the deforming surface correctly.

What decides quality is correspondence, not the arithmetic. The arithmetic is one subtraction of t, then two multiplies and one add per coordinate — trivial next to the work of finding good correspondence.

figure.caption: Both branches read the same t = 0.3, so outline and colour move together: the control point travels from A(0, 0) to (30, 12) while the colours mix 0.7 of the source with 0.3 of the target. Feed the two branches different t values and the shape and its colour pull apart.

spec.title: One t for both jobs
spec.aria: A matched control pair A(0,0) and B(100,40) feeds two parallel branches that both use t = 0.3: a warp that puts the point at (30, 12) and a cross-dissolve weighing 0.7 of the source against 0.3 of the target, the two branches joining into the frame at t = 0.3.

examples.question: Two images have matched control points. In the source image a control point sits at A(0, 0); in the target image the matched point sits at B(100, 40). Coordinates are in pixels, origin at the top-left. Find the intermediate position at t = 0.3, and give the weights the cross-dissolve uses at that same instant.
steps: t = 0.3, so the source weight is 1 − t = 0.7 and the target weight is t = 0.3.
The interpolated control point is P(0.3) = (30, 12).

The control point sits 30 px right and 12 px down from the source position, and 70 px left and 28 px up from the target position (about 75 px away in a straight line) — as expected, since t = 0.3 is nearer the source.
Cross-dissolve weights: source 0.7, target 0.3. They add to 1.0, so brightness is preserved.
A pixel colour there is C = 0.7·C_A + 0.3·C_B, per channel.
examples.answer: The control point is at (30, 12), and the cross-dissolve uses 0.7 of the warped source and 0.3 of the warped target.
examples.check:
ax, ay = 0.0, 0.0
bx, by = 100.0, 40.0
t = 0.3

x = (1 - t) * ax + t * bx
y = (1 - t) * ay + t * by
w_source = 1 - t
w_target = t

print(round(x, 6))
print(round(y, 6))
print(round(w_source, 6))
print(round(w_target, 6))

traps: Calling a plain cross-dissolve a morph. A fade moves no geometry; marks are awarded for naming the warp as well.
Mismatched or too few control points. The mesh folds or tears, and the examiner's favourite phrase is 'correspondence is the hard part'.

Confusing the two weights. The source uses (1 − t) and the target uses t. Writing t and t makes the total weight 2t, so the frames are dark near t = 0 and t = 1 and correct only at t = 0.5, and the colour crosses over on a wrong, non-linear schedule; writing t and (1 − t) reverses the direction.
Using one t for the warp and another for the dissolve, so outline and colour drift apart.
Forward warping leaves holes when control points spread apart; inverse warping with bilinear sampling is the standard fix, not a bigger mesh alone.

quiz.q: Name the two ingredients of an image morph and say what joins them.
quiz.a: A geometric warp and a cross-dissolve, joined by the correspondence between matched control points or mesh nodes.

quiz.q: What do t = 0 and t = 1 produce?
quiz.a: t = 0 gives the source image exactly; t = 1 gives the target image exactly.

quiz.q: Why is inverse warping preferred over forward warping?
quiz.a: Forward warping pushes source pixels forward and leaves holes where points spread apart, and loses pixels where they bunch. Inverse warping visits every output pixel, so each gets exactly one value; it needs the map inverted once and bilinear sampling for smoothness.

quiz.q: A control point at A(20, 10) is matched to B(60, 50). Find its position at t = 0.25 and the dissolve weights at that instant.
One colour channel has C_A = 200 and C_B = 40 at t = 0.6. Give the dissolved value.
A morph looks right in the middle frames but the outline shivers throughout. Give the likely cause and one check.
quiz.a: The likely cause is poor correspondence — wrongly paired or too few control points, so the mesh folds locally. Check the pairing by moving t slowly and watching each control point: a shiver or fold points to a bad pair, so add or correct control points there.

quiz.q: Why must a 3D vertex morph have identical topology on both meshes, and what do you do if it does not?
quiz.a: The formula pairs vertex i of A with vertex i of B, so the two meshes need the same vertex count and the same faces in the same order; otherwise triangles connect wrongly and the surface tears. Fix it by remeshing one model onto the other, or by morphing through an intermediate mesh with the required topology.

quiz.q: Why should the two dissolve weights add to 1?
quiz.a: So a flat region keeps constant brightness across the morph; weights that sum above 1 brighten the middle frames, below 1 they darken them.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research morphing is mostly research on correspondence: face landmarks, optical flow and learned warping fields now supply the matched points that a person once clicked by hand. Film and game studios drive facial animation with blendshapes, which are many vertex morphs blended at once. Morphing between 3D scans, and between the latent codes of generative models, is an active area. Search for field morphing, optical flow warping and blendshapes to go further.
